message.content: Thesis: It would be a clever move in principle, but it is only in character for Hux if he is desperate, cornered, and trying to fake competence against the Knights of Ren. Assuming you mean putting the disguised detonator on display as bait, the idea works best if Hux is not the one who originally created the scheme, but rather someone who seizes on it in a panic. Hux is not naturally a patient mastermind; he is theatrical, insecure, eager to please, and often overconfident beyond his abilities. So he could absolutely try to use a “holocron” as a trap if he believes it will make him look indispensable to Kylo, Snoke, or the First Order leadership. The move would be in character if it is clumsy, dramatic, and slightly too obvious—Hux would probably announce it, display it prominently, and expect everyone to admire his brilliance instead of realizing how risky it is. Thesis: If the Knights of Ren become a third party, a thermal detonator disguised as a holocron is a strong bait because it targets their interest in ancient power, Jedi secrets, and mysterious relics. The Knights of Ren are not simply another First Order unit; they have their own cultural and historical appeal. They are drawn to old power, dark legacy, and anything connected to the Jedi. A fake holocron would appeal directly to that obsession. Hux could theoretically use it to lure them into a trap, provoke them into revealing their intentions, or make them believe the First Order is hiding or hoarding Jedi artifacts. That makes the idea tactically interesting: it weaponizes the Knights’ reputation and their attraction to relics rather than relying on brute force. Thesis: The idea is in character only if it reflects Hux’s weakness, insecurity, and need to appear useful, not if it turns him into a calculating schemer. If the scene shows Hux calmly planning the deception over weeks, hiding the truth from Kylo, and manipulating everyone with quiet intelligence, that would be less in character. But if he is frightened by the Knights of Ren, worried that they will turn against the First Order, or desperate to prove himself after a failure, the move becomes much more plausible. Hux might not fully understand what he is doing. He might trust a technician or officer to build the fake holocron, then present it with exaggerated confidence. The best version of this idea is not Hux being brilliant; it is Hux pretending to be brilliant while the danger of the scheme slowly closes in on him. Thesis: It is clever as a narrative device if the disguised detonator has a specific purpose, such as drawing the Knights away, creating a false Jedi attack, or punishing perceived traitors. The move becomes especially effective if Hux uses it to cover up a larger weakness. For example, if the Knights of Ren begin investigating the First Order’s Jedi-related crimes, Hux might plant the fake holocron to make them suspect a third-party Jedi cell, an internal spy, or a rival faction. It could also be used as a trap for Kylo or his own superiors if Hux begins to see that he is expendable. In that case, the disguised detonator is not just a joke or a cheap trap; it is a piece of insurance, a bluff, or a desperate attempt to shift blame. The cleverness comes from how the object reflects First Order paranoia: everyone wants Jedi power, and everyone fears what that power can do to them. Thesis: The best version is that Hux makes a “clever” move that is only half clever: theatrical, dangerous, poorly disguised, and ultimately exposing his fear rather than his competence. So yes, it can be both in character and clever if played with the right tone. Hux could put the fake holocron on a pedestal, in a containment field, or inside a sealed display case labeled as a recovered Jedi artifact. He might believe it will intimidate the Knights, distract them, or make him look like he has recovered something valuable. But the audience should understand that the disguise is flimsy, the detonator is unstable, and Hux may have no real control over the outcome. The funniest and most character-driven result would be that the “clever move” immediately backfires: the Knights smell the lie, the detonator is about to blow up, or Hux accidentally reveals that the “holocron” is just a bomb. That would preserve his voice, respect the danger of the Knights as a third party, and give the scene both wit and tension.
